Compute variance decomposition (BS and WS components)

Source: R/strata_eval_functions.R
compute_variance_decomposition.Rd

Computes the between-strata (BS) and within-strata (WS) variance components of the residuals. These components are related to the variance reduction from stratified sampling as described in Theorem 3.2 of the manuscript.

compute_variance_decomposition(dat, Z = "Z", strata = NULL, n_code = NULL)

Arguments

dat

Data frame with Yobs, Yhat columns

Z

Character string specifying the treatment indicator column name, or NULL to ignore treatment groups. Default is "Z".

strata

Stratification variable. Can be a vector of stratum assignments (same length as nrow(dat)) or NULL if dat already contains a column named "strata".

n_code

Optional. Total number of units to be sampled for coding. If provided, the function computes the exact BS and WS terms from Theorem 3.2 which depend on the sampling fraction. If NULL (default), computes simplified population-level variance decomposition components that serve as proxies.

Value

If Z is specified (treatment/control), returns a list with:

by_arm

Data frame with decomposition for each treatment arm.

overall

Data frame with overall decomposition (summed over arms).

If Z is NULL, returns a single data frame with the decomposition. See details for the specific components included in each case.

Details

The variance reduction from stratified sampling (Theorem 3.2) is:

$$Var(\hat{\tau}_{SRS}) - Var(\hat{\tau}_{strat}) = BS - WS$$

Simplified (population-level) decomposition (when n_code = NULL):

This computes the standard ANOVA-style decomposition of residual variance:

  • BS = sum_k w_k * (mean_resid_k - grand_mean)^2

  • WS = sum_k w_k * var_resid_k

where w_k = N_zk / N_z is the stratum weight. This satisfies: $$Var(resid) = BS + WS$$

These simplified components serve as useful diagnostics:

  • Large BS suggests systematic differences in prediction bias across strata, which stratification can exploit.

  • Heterogeneous within-stratum variances (captured by var_ratio) suggest potential benefit from optimal allocation.

Exact Theorem 3.2 decomposition (when n_code is provided):

The exact formulas incorporate finite population corrections and sampling fractions. The BS term from Theorem 3.2 is: $$BS = sum_k [ (N_z - n_z)/N_z * N_zk / (n_z(N_z-1)) * (mean_resid_k - grand_mean)^2 ]$$

The WS term is more complex and depends on the sampling design. Under proportional allocation, WS is approximately zero. Under optimal allocation (oversampling high-variance strata), WS can become negative, providing additional variance reduction.

The returned decomposition includes:

BS

Between-strata variance component. Measures how much stratum mean residuals differ from the grand mean. Larger values indicate greater potential benefit from stratification.

WS

Within-strata variance component. Weighted average of within-stratum residual variances. Under proportional allocation, this term is typically small and positive. NOTE: The exact WS term from Theorem 3.2 can be negative under optimal allocation (oversampling high-variance strata), but the simplified population version computed here is always positive.

BS_minus_WS

The difference BS - WS, which approximates the variance reduction from stratified sampling vs. SRS. Positive values indicate stratification reduces variance.

See also

evaluate_stratification for computing stratification quality metrics, plot_strata_residuals for visualization.
